reason: Branches can bear cobwebby (arachnoid) hairs, and the examples describe that.
A leaf margin can be curled or rolled, and the examples fit.
This is a tube-type part (perianth or corolla tube), and a tube has a diameter. The examples give diameter at the base or throat.
Tube length is routine in floras. 'Longer than spathe' is a comparison, but a rule can handle that.
PATO 'unstructured' is the wrong reading of 'subentire', which describes a margin or apex outline. A margin or apex quality, not unstructured, would be needed.
The examples are spurs and appendices, which belong to a different part. 'Petal' is the wrong bearer, so the pair exists only through a wrong reading.
A lamina lobe or segment can be oblong.
An anther cap can be narrowed or tapered. The examples include the negated 'not narrowed toward apex', which a rule would have to handle.
Thickness is meaningful for this part, and the examples give measurements.
Stipels can be deciduous or caducous.
A petiolule can be scaly (lepidote).
Margins of flat parts can be fimbriate.
A limb (flower or leaf part) can be erect, and the examples fit.

The examples are hirsute, villous and puberulent, which are specific hair types. 'Pilosity' is a generic attribute and the part is unclear. A rule would map specific hair terms to their own PATO values, not to the attribute.
A fruit pedicel can be robust (stout).
'Sinus with a small tooth' describes a tooth in the sinus, not a dentate sinus. The wrong reading puts the quality on the wrong bearer, so a tooth should be annotated as a part.
A labellum or lobe can be rhomboid. The bearer is a flower-part class, and the examples fit.
'Prolonged into tendrils' and 'without tendrils' say the peduncle bears or ends in a tendril. That is a part-of relation, not a tendrilous quality, and the negation makes it worse.
Pappus elements (bristles) can be deciduous.
Stem nodes can be thickened.
The hypochile has a shape (saccate, globose, concave), and the attribute is correct.
A lip or lobe can be T-shaped. The examples are correct.
Position is meaningful for a pollen cone (axillary). It would be better to use a specific position value.
Filaments can be obsolete or vestigial.
A count of intramarginal veins is meaningful, and the amount quality fits a count.
A spathe can be suberect (semi-erect). 'Erect-spreading' is a mixed term, but the pair itself is fine.
A scale leaf has a width.
An ovule has a shape.
A utricle can be globose (spherical).
Parts such as a tube, mouth or blade base can be constricted. The bearer is a tube-type class, so this fits.
A notched connective is possible, but 'ensellé' means saddle-shaped, which is a different reading. A rule would need to tell French 'ensellé' from English 'notched'.
Lobes can be small, and the examples fit.
A petal apex can be incised (cut).
Oil glands can be inconspicuous, which fits 'not visible'.
A sheath apex may be arched. The bearer is the sheath, not its apex. A rule would need to move apex-bearing text to an apex part.
An auricle can be large.
An internode can have a mealy or powdery coating. Some examples are negated ('not white powdery'), so negation needs handling.
Gemmae occur in clusters (aggregated).
A stigma can be twisted.
The examples are about the lips and the middle lobe, not the corolla as a whole. A rule would need to move the quality to the lip or lobe when the text names it.
'Ellipsoid' was read as prolate. An ellipsoid is not the same as a prolate spheroid, so the PATO term means something else.
A sporangium can be globose (spherical).
A higher-order inflorescence axis (branch) can be long. 'Longer than nutlet' is a comparison, but the pair is fine.
An anther cap can be glabrous.
Pseudobulbs can be globose.
Breadth is meaningful here. Most examples give a measurement, and 'broader than long' is a comparison.
The examples ('base enlarged', 'apex enlarged') are about a region of the part, not the whole part. A rule would need to find the region and attach the quality to it.
A peristome can be short.
Corona scales and lobes can be lanceolate.
'Hyaline' means thin and translucent, and it often applies to margins or the orifice, not the whole utricle. A rule would need to attach it to the named part.
A utricle surface can be hispid. 'Margins hispid' is a part-specific case, but the pair is acceptable.
The examples are about the base or apex narrowing (stipe, beak), not the whole utricle. A rule would need to assign the quality to the base or apex.
A spikelet can be small.
Branches, arms or other thread-like parts can be filiform.
An epicalyx bract or lobe has a 2-D shape.
'Fascicled indumentum' means hairs in tufts, while 'branches fascicled' means branches in bundles. A rule would need to tell hair arrangement from branch arrangement.
A caryopsis has a 2-D outline shape.
A perianth tube can be obconical.
Surfaces can be sericeous (silky hairs), and the examples fit.
'Septate' (divided by partitions) is read as 'split'. This is a wrong reading. Also, a short shoot interior is not a normal bearer, and the text probably describes a pith or stem part.
